Conditions

Presentation Objectives  
Understand the essential anatomy and physiology of the external and middle ear.  
Master the systematic approach to history taking and physical ear examination.  
Differentiate between earwax impaction, otitis externa, and otitis media.  
Review pharmacological management options for common ear conditions.  
Identify "Red Flag" symptoms requiring urgent medical referral.

External Auditory Meatus (EAM)  
The EAM is an S-shaped canal approximately 2.5 cm long in  
adults:  
•
Outer 1/3: Cartilaginous, containing hair follicles and  
ceruminous glands.  
Inner 2/3: Bony structure, very sensitive to pain and  
•
pressure.  
•
Protective Barrier: Curvature and wax production  
protect the delicate tympanic membrane.  
Physiology of Earwax (Cerumen)  
Protection  
Antimicrobial  
Self-Cleaning  
Traps dust, debris, and  
microorganisms. Repels water  
from the eardrum.  
Slightly acidic medium helps  
protect against bacterial and  
fungal infections.  
Epithelial migration moves wax  
outwards from the tympanic  
membrane to the exterior.  
02. Clinical  
Assessment  
The Patient History: Key Questions  
Symptom Onset  
Associated Signs  
Was the hearing loss sudden (trauma/infection) or  
gradual (wax impaction)?  
Is there discharge? (Mucinous suggests middle ear  
involvement).  
Is there pain? Does it worsen with ear movement?  
Are there systemic symptoms like fever or malaise?  
Physical Examination (Steps 1-3)  
1. Hygiene: Wash hands and explain the procedure to the  
patient.  
2. Inspection: Check the pinna and EAM for redness,  
swelling, or discharge.  
3. Palpation: Apply pressure to the tragus and pull the  
pinna to assess for tenderness.  
Physical Examination (Steps 4-5)  
4. Otoscopy Preparation: Select the largest speculum  
that fits comfortably in the canal.  
5. Visualization: Gently pull the pinna up and back to  
straighten the canal for viewing.  
Healthy Otoscopic Landmarks  
Tympanic Membrane  
A normal eardrum appears as a translucent, pearly-gray  
membrane. Key features to observe:  
•
The handle of the Malleus.  
•
The Cone of Light (reflex).  
•
Absence of redness, bulging, or perforation.

03. Cerumen  
Impaction  
The Burden of Earwax  
Procedures Annually  
Earwax removal is the most common ENT procedure in UK primary care, impacting ~4%  
of the population annually. It is a major cause of conductive hearing loss.  
2.3M  
Features of Wax Impaction  
Objective Findings  
Otoscopy reveals a solid mass of wax obstructing the  
canal, preventing visualization of the eardrum.  
Subjective Symptoms  
Gradual hearing loss, a sense of "fullness," discomfort,  
and occasionally tinnitus or dizziness.  
Management: Cerumenolytics  
Oil-based  
Water-based  
Peroxide-based  
Olive or Almond oil. Softens the  
wax to facilitate natural migration.  
Sodium bicarbonate. Breaks down  
the wax into smaller fragments.  
Hydrogen peroxide. Releases  
oxygen bubbles to disintegrate  
wax mass.  
Practical Tips:  
Administering Drops  
Warm the Bottle: Roll between palms for 2-3 mins to  
reach body temperature.  
Positioning: Tilt head sideways or lie down with the  
affected ear up.  
Dwell Time: Maintain the position for 5-10 mins after  
application.  
04. Otitis  
Externa  
Definition & Epidemiology  
Annual Incidence  
Otitis externa is inflammation of the external ear canal skin. Known as "Swimmer's Ear," it is highly  
1%  
prevalent in humid environments and during summer months.  
Pathogenesis & Microbes  
Primary Pathogens  
Risk Factors  
Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus are  
the most common bacterial causes. Fungal causes  
(Otomycosis) include Aspergillus.  
Moisture (swimming), micro-trauma (cotton buds),  
and underlying skin conditions (eczema, seborrhoea).  
Clinical Presentation of OE  
Signs & Symptoms  
•
Severe itch and progressive ear pain.  
•
Erythema and edema of the ear canal.  
•
Debris or discharge in the canal.  
•
Pathognomonic: Pain on traction of the pinna.  
Management: Acetic Acid (2%)  
Cochrane Review & Guidance  
Evidence: Reviews show no single topical agent is significantly superior, but combination preparations (steroid + antibiotic) are  
highly effective.  
Prohibition: Advise patients to avoid all insertion of foreign objects (cotton buds) into the canal.  
Dry Ear Precautions: Keep the ear dry during treatment and for 7-10 days after symptoms resolve.

Trauma & Foreign Bodies  
Ear Trauma  
Foreign Bodies  
Perforation  
Lacerations or haematomas from

Common in children (beads,  
insects). Symptoms include  
irritation and secondary infection.  
Rupture of the tympanic  
membrane due to trauma or severe  
infection. Requires referral.  
Malignancy Spotlight  
Malignant Tumors  
Rare but serious. Should be suspected if an ulcerated area on  
the pinna fails to heal or if blood-stained discharge is present in  
an older patient.  
Urgent referral is mandatory for non-healing lesions.  
Referral Criteria: Red Flags  
Severe Systemic Symptoms: Fever, malaise, or profound swelling behind the ear.  
Hearing Loss: Sudden onset hearing loss not clearly attributable to wax.  
Emergency Symptoms: Dizziness or tinnitus accompanied by deep ear pain.  
Children: All children with ear pain or suspected foreign bodies must be referred.
